name: Muong
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.verdict: a source was named but could not be reached

sources.citation: Phan, John D. 2012. Mường is not a subgroup: phonological evidence for a paraphyletic taxon in the Viet-Muong sub-family. Mon-Khmer Studies 40: 1-18.
sources.note: Historical-phonological; the 'stress' hits in the saved volume belong to other MKS 40 articles, not to Muong.

sources.citation: Barker, Miriam A. 1993. Bibliography of Mường and other Vietic language groups, with notes. Mon-Khmer Studies 23: 197-243.
sources.note: Page-image scan, scanned. Annotated bibliography; no entry mentions stress. Confirms Barker 1968 'The phonemes of Mương' (SiL 20: 59-62; Mường Khến dialect; 'phonemes of monosyllables: consonants, vowels, tones and sequence limitations'), Sokolovskaya & Nguyen Van Tai 1987 ('in Russian; includes a grammatical description'), Nguyen Van Tai 1983 graduate thesis (~60 varieties).

sources.citation: Nguyễn, Minh-Châu. 2021. Glottalization, tonal contrasts and intonation: an experimental study of the Kim Thuong dialect of Muong. PhD thesis, Université Sorbonne Nouvelle - Paris 3. 351 pp.
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: open copy online
sources.note: Nothing about Muong word stress anywhere (all 'stress'/'accent' hits are generic prosody theory). Places Muong among languages with lexical tones (p. 11); 'Muong is a monosyllabic language, in the sense that a syllable = a morpheme = a word' (p. 69); function words carry lexical tone like content words (p. 76); tone inventory of Kim Thuong Muong in sect. 2.7.3 (pp. 54-60).

sources.citation: Nguyễn, Minh-Châu. 2016. The tone system of Kim Thượng Mường: an experimental study of fundamental frequency, duration, and phonation types. MA thesis, University of Social Sciences and Humanities, Hanoi. 164 pp.
sources.note: No stress statement. p. 21: 'Like Vietnamese, Mường is a strictly monosyllabic language from a phonological point of view: the syllable is the domain of tone'; disyllables exist in the lexicon through collocation/disyllabification.

sources.citation: Nguyễn, Minh-Châu, Lise Crevier-Buchman, Alexis Michaud & Didier Demolin. 2019. A glottalized tone in Muong (Vietic): a pilot study based on audio and electroglottographic recordings. Proc. ICPhS 2019, Melbourne. 6 pp.
sources.note: Silent on stress; tone/phonation study of monosyllabic target items.

sources.citation: Ferlus, Michel. 1998. Les systèmes de tons dans les langues viet-muong. Diachronica 15(1): 1-27 (HAL author version).
sources.note: Comparative tonogenesis; no statement on stress (only 'accent grave' as a diacritic).

sources.citation: Thompson, Laurence C. (1976). Proto-Viet-Muong Phonology. In Austroasiatic Studies. Honolulu: The University Press of Hawaii. pp. 1113-1204.
sources.note: Muong is not in the catalog and has no existing stress statements; this work adds only a tone inventory for Muong Khen and is silent on word stress, consistent with the earlier-read sources in this folder (Nguyen 2016/2021: strictly monosyllabic tone language, no stress statement).

sources.citation: Wikipedia (en, vi) 'Muong language' / 'Tiếng Mường'
sources.note: Tonal (5-6 tones), syllable structure; explicitly nothing about stress. Cite Nguyen Van Tai 1982/2005, Nguyen 2021, the 2002 Mường-Việt dictionary.
